svg.title: Microscopy
svg.desc: Magnification & resolution: Magnification: image enlargement. Resolution: distinguish two close points as separate. Enlarging a blurred photograph adds no detail. Bigger does not mean clearer. Light & electron: Light microscopes: show cells and visible structures. Electron microscopes: much greater magnification and resolving power. They reveal finer sub-cellular detail. Size formulae: Magnification = image ÷ actual Actual size = image ÷ magnification Image size = actual × magnification Convert to the same units first. Magnification has no unit. Image and actual sizes do. Worked magnification: Image: 30 mm. Actual cell: 60 µm. 30 × 1,000 = 30,000 µm. 30,000 ÷ 60 = ×500. Microscope total = eyepiece × objective. ×10 × ×40 = ×400. Drawing magnification depends on drawing size, not automatically the microscope setting. Units & standard form: 1 cm = 10 mm 1 mm = 1,000 µm 1 µm = 1,000 nm 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m. 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. Larger to smaller units: multiply. Reverse: divide. Standard form: a × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ a < 10. 0.000060 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m. Scale & area: 20 µm ÷ 2 µm = 10: one order of magnitude. Convert units before comparing. A scale bar shows actual distance. Compare image length with the bar. Estimate sizes or areas when boundaries are unclear. For similar shapes, doubling length makes area four times larger. State the assumption. Prepare the slide: Observe plant and animal cells. Thin onion epidermis, water and a suitable stain such as iodine. Lower the coverslip at an angle to reduce air bubbles. Thin tissue lets light through and avoids overlap. Use teacher-approved animal samples. Handle glass, stains and samples safely. Focus & draw: Start with the lowest-power objective. Coarse then fine focus. Centre cells, increase magnification and use fine focus. Clear pencil outlines. No shading. Label visible structures. Add a magnification scale or scale bar. Draw what you observe, not just what you remember.
